claims.text: The initial W–Cu composite contains W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
A conventional W–Cu composite exhibits phase separation and interfacial voids.
A trace amount of Ni can be introduced during consolidation or sintering as a single intervention.
Ni added during W–Cu consolidation or sintering will segregate to the W–Cu interface.
Interfacial dopant segregation will lower the W–Cu interfacial energy.
The reactive dopant will improve wettability between W and Cu.
The dopant will catalyze formation of a stable intermetallic bonding layer at the W–Cu interface.
The dopant-induced interfacial layer will be ultra-thin and continuously distributed.
The interfacial bonding layer will suppress phase separation during processing and service.
The interfacial bonding layer will reduce interfacial void formation during processing and service.
Reduced interfacial voids and phase separation will improve thermal conductivity relative to untreated W–Cu.
The doped composite will maintain structural integrity under irradiation and high heat flux.
Interfacial voids and phase separation in untreated W–Cu result in lower thermal conductivity and compromised structural performance.
The intervention will remain effective under high thermal gradients and irradiation typical of W-based plasma-facing material/Cu-based cooling-component joints.
The optimal dopant concentration, intermetallic-layer characteristics, and magnitude of thermal-conductivity improvement remain uncertain and may depend on processing parameters.
